qualitative_transfer_notes: A flat continuation may be vulnerable to an unobserved level shift later in the forecast horizon; this is a hypothesis, not an established cause.
The supplied context does not establish a relationship between the target and weather information, so that information may not have helped anticipate changes.

Treat this as a caution when the target is unnamed or its relationship to supplied covariates is unestablished, the visible history contains abrupt level shifts, and the forecast holds a flat level over a long irregular horizon.
Use only when prediction-time evidence supports describing the recent level as steady; retain uncertainty about possible shifts rather than treating a plateau as proof of persistence.
Do not apply when prediction-time evidence establishes a reliable target relationship or a clear trend that supports a different forecast shape.
Exclude text or covariates whose timing, alignment, relevance, or source quality is too uncertain to inform the forecast.

Post-hoc case-local empirical update: The first B forecast added detailed oscillations over a long irregular horizon and had worse absolute error than the flat A baseline. When intervals are irregular and the target is undefined, do not invent a future oscillation schedule. Prefer a stable level supported by the dominant recent history; only add variation when the pre-target sequence establishes a repeatable pattern.
